title: How a Jataka works
hook: each tale has a present story, a past story, and a last line saying who each character was

segments.voice: Yesterday, the songs closed, and the elders sang one last time. Your line was the elders sang. Today, a new block begins: the longer Jataka tales.

The talkative tortoise was Kokalika. The wise minister was the Bodhisatta. That's how one tale ends, in the Jataka, the great collection of stories about the Buddha's past lives. Two sentences, and suddenly a fable about a tortoise is also about a monk the listeners knew. Before the longer tales of the coming weeks, today is about the frame they share. Learn the frame once, and the tales that follow get easier to read.
screen: `THE TORTOISE WAS KOKALIKA.` → `A FABLE ABOUT SOMEONE THEY KNEW.` → `LEARN THE FRAME ONCE.`

segments.voice: First, a story in the present. A tale opens in the Buddha's own lifetime, with something that has just happened among the monks. In the tortoise tale, a monk named Kokalika has come to ruin through his own careless tongue, and the monks are talking about it. The Buddha says: this isn't the first time his tongue has brought him down. Second, a story in the past. Long ago, when a king reigned in Benares, the Bodhisatta, the Buddha in an earlier life, was that king's minister. The king talked without stopping. Meanwhile, a tortoise made friends with two young geese, and they offered to fly him home with them, if he'd bite the middle of a stick and keep his mouth shut. Up they went. Villagers below shouted and laughed at the sight. The tortoise opened his mouth to answer back, let go of the stick, and fell into the king's courtyard. The minister used the broken tortoise to teach the king to talk less. Third, the verses. Somewhere in the tale, someone speaks a short verse, here the Bodhisatta to his king, the lesson pressed into a few lines. Fourth, who was who. Then the Buddha connects the two stories. The tortoise was Kokalika. The minister was the Bodhisatta. That last line is the hinge. It turns an old fable into a mirror: the same habits, the same people, coming round again. When you read a Jataka, you can start at the end. The last line tells you who to watch.
screen: `A STORY IN THE PRESENT.` · `A STORY IN THE PAST.` · `A VERSE WITH THE LESSON.` · `THE LAST LINE IS THE HINGE.` · then, large: `WHO WAS WHO.`

segments.voice: Hold the tortoise tale's last line: the tortoise was Kokalika; the wise minister was the Bodhisatta. Then bring up one small moment from your week, a conversation, a mistake, a kindness, tell it as a tiny fable in your mind, and give it a last line: who was the tortoise there, and who was the wise minister? You might be both, so just see who was who, without judging.
Samodhana. The connection: the closing part of a Jataka where the Buddha says who was who, after a story in the present and a story in the past. Today's word.
Your line: who was who. The ending is the key to the whole tale. That's day eight hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Jataka tales are retold, painted and performed in Theravada communities, and in the collection each tale closes by saying who each character was.

chat.says: How do you know who's who in those old stories of the Buddha's past lives?
options: At the end, the Buddha says who was who: the tortoise was Kokalika.
The first line tells you, before the story about the past begins.
You can't; the stories never say who the animals really were.
chat.meaning: A Jataka ends with the samodhana: the Buddha links the past story to the present, saying who each character was.

Kokalika.meaning: a monk ruined by his own careless tongue

Jataka.meaning: a story of one of the Buddha's past lives

Bodhisatta.meaning: the Buddha in an earlier life, on the way to awakening

Benares.meaning: an old Indian city, today's Varanasi

Samodhana.meaning: the connection: the closing line saying who was who

notes: Paraphrased; nothing quoted. Cowell's translation (1895–1907) is public domain but not on the validator's list, so it is not quoted.

Jataka 215: confirm the present story (Kokalika ruined through his speech; the Buddha says it wasn't the first time), the past story (talkative king of Benares, the Bodhisatta as his minister; the tortoise, the two young geese, the stick, villagers jeering, the fall into the courtyard; the king learning to speak less) and the identification (Kokalika the tortoise, the Bodhisatta the minister).
The hook says 'the great collection'; that is a description, not a count. Confirm acceptable.

Trapdoor floor 3 states that the canonical Jataka contains only the verses, with the prose (present story, past story, samodhana) in the commentary. This is the standard scholarly account; a Keeper should confirm the wording.
The teach describes the verses as 'often the Bodhisatta' speaking; in Jataka 215 the Bodhisatta speaks verses to the king. Confirm.
howItsDone: confirm that tellings traditionally end with the identification, and that temple murals and festival performances are fair general description.
Original: समोधान (samodhana). Confirm Devanagari and stress.
